module_title: Consumer Protection and No-Fault Liability: Foundational Concepts
introduction: This foundational level introduces two massive pillars of civil law: the statutory protection of consumers under the Consumer Protection Act (CPA) 2019, and the tortious concepts of 'No-Fault Liability' where a person can be held liable even without being negligent.

core_concepts.title: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019
core_concepts.description:
The CPA 2019 replaced the outdated 1986 Act to modernize consumer rights for the digital age. 
- Who is a Consumer?: Any person who buys goods or hires services for consideration (money). Crucially, it EXCLUDES anyone who buys goods for resale or commercial purposes.
- Scope: It explicitly covers all transactions, including offline, online (e-commerce), teleshopping, and direct selling.

core_concepts.title: The Six Consumer Rights
core_concepts.description:
The CPA legally guarantees 6 fundamental rights:
1. Right to Safety (protection against hazardous goods).
2. Right to Information (knowing quality, quantity, price).
3. Right to Choose (access to a variety of goods at competitive prices).
4. Right to be Heard (representation in consumer forums).
5. Right to seek Redressal (against unfair trade practices).
6. Right to Consumer Education.

core_concepts.title: Strict Liability (The Rule in Rylands v. Fletcher)
core_concepts.description:
In tort law, usually, you must prove 'fault' (negligence) to get compensation. Strict Liability is an exception. 
- The Rule (1868): If a person brings a dangerous thing onto their land for a non-natural use, and it escapes and causes harm, they are strictly liable for the damage, even if they took all reasonable care to prevent the escape. 
- It is called 'No-Fault Liability' because the defendant's intention or care doesn't matter.

core_concepts.title: Absolute Liability (The Rule in M.C. Mehta v. Union of India)
core_concepts.description:
India created its own, harsher version of Strict Liability following industrial disasters. 
- The Rule (1987): If an enterprise is engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous activity and harm results to anyone on account of an accident in the operation of such activity, the enterprise is absolutely liable to compensate all those affected. 
- The Difference: Unlike Strict Liability, Absolute Liability has ZERO exceptions or defenses.

important_entities.name: CCPA (Central Consumer Protection Authority)
important_entities.key_fact: The regulatory watchdog created by the CPA 2019.
important_entities.significance: Unlike consumer courts which wait for a complaint, the CCPA can take *suo motu* action (on its own), conduct investigations into misleading advertisements, order the recall of hazardous goods, and impose heavy penalties.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Examiners will ask: 'A patient receives free treatment at a government hospital and suffers due to medical negligence. Can they sue under the CPA?' The answer is NO. The CPA explicitly states that 'services rendered free of charge' are outside the definition of a consumer transaction. The patient must sue in traditional tort (negligence), not under the CPA.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: Strict = Rylands v. Fletcher (England); Absolute = M.C. Mehta (India)
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Always link the 1868 British case to Strict Liability and the 1987 Indian Oleum Gas Leak case to Absolute Liability.

exam_strategy_tips: Whenever an exam asks 'Which liability principle allows absolutely NO defenses?', the answer is **Absolute Liability** [1.2.3].
